text: Knowing that qubits drift and get recalibrated is only useful if you can actually read the data a provider publishes and use it to make a real decision. This lesson is hands-on: what's actually in a calibration report, and how a practitioner uses it.

Providers that give users access to real hardware typically publish, at minimum: per-qubit T1, the energy relaxation time; per-qubit T2, the dephasing time, both usually in microseconds; readout error, the probability of measuring a qubit's state incorrectly; per-qubit single-gate error rates; per-edge two-qubit gate error rates, which vary noticeably from one connection to another; gate times, since a circuit takes real time to run and decoherence happens during that time; and a last-calibrated timestamp.

A chip is not uniform. On any real device, some qubits have longer T1 and T2 than others, some have worse readout error, and the connections between qubits have a wide spread of two-qubit error rates — often spanning more than a factor of two between the best and worst edges on the same chip. That means two circuits running on the same device can see meaningfully different real-world performance depending entirely on which physical qubits and connections they land on.

A practical workflow: first, identify the connectivity your circuit actually needs — which qubits must interact, and in what pattern. Second, scan edge error rates for connections matching that pattern, and preferentially map onto the lowest-error edges available. Third, check T1 and T2 against your circuit's expected runtime — if total gate depth times typical gate time approaches a meaningful fraction of coherence time, expect decoherence to show up directly in your results. Fourth, check readout error specifically on the qubits you'll actually measure. Most toolchains automate a version of this, but understanding the underlying data lets you sanity-check or override that automated choice.

That closes out control systems and calibration. Next chapter turns everything you've learned about qubit count, fidelity, and connectivity into the discipline of reading a vendor's hardware claims critically — starting with the metrics that actually matter.
